[[File:Assouad dimension.svg|thumb|right|350px|The Assouad dimension of the [[Sierpiński triangle]] is equal to its [[Hausdorff dimension]], <math>\alpha = \frac{\log(3)}{\log(2)}</math>.  In the illustration, we see that for a particular choice of {{mvar|r}}, {{mvar|R}}, and {{mvar|x}}, <math display="block"> N_{r}(B_{R}(x) \cap E) = 3 = 2^\alpha = \left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^{\alpha}.</math> For other choices, the constant {{mvar|C}} may be greater than 1, but is still bounded.]]

In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in [[fractal geometry]] &mdash; the '''Assouad dimension''' is a definition of [[fractal dimension]] for subsets of a [[metric space]].  It was introduced by [[Patrice Assouad]] in his 1977 [[PhD]] [[thesis]] and later published in 1979,<ref>{{cite journal
| last = Assouad
| first = Patrice
| title = Étude d'une dimension métrique liée à la possibilité de plongements dans '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>
| journal = Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Série A-B
| volume = 288
| year = 1979
| issue = 15
| pages = A731&ndash;A734
| language=fr
| issn = 0151-0509}} {{MathSciNet|id=532401}}</ref> although the same notion had been studied in 1928 by [[Georges Bouligand]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last=Bouligand
| first=Georges <!--M. stands for Monsieur-->
| author-link=Georges Bouligand
| year=1928
| title=Ensembles impropres et nombre dimensionnel
| journal=Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques
| volume=52
| pages=320–344
| language=fr
| url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k486279t/f406.item}}</ref>  As well as being used to study fractals, the Assouad dimension has also been used to study [[quasiconformal mapping]]s and [[embedding|embeddability problems]].

==Definition==

{{Quote|The ''Assouad dimension''<!--italics in original--> of <math>X, d_A(X)</math>, is the infimum of all <math>s</math> such that <math>(X, \varsigma)</math> is <math>(M, s)</math>-homogeneous for some <math>M \ge 1</math>.<ref>{{cite book| last=Robinson |first=James C. |year=2010 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qFyXxiKfA9UC&dq=Assouad+dimension&pg=PA83 |title=Dimensions, Embeddings, and Attractors |page=85 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781139495189}}</ref>}}

Let <math>(X, d)</math> be a [[metric space]], and let {{mvar|E}} be a non-empty subset of {{mvar|X}}.  For {{math|''r'' > 0}}, let <math>N_{r}(E)</math> denote the least number of metric [[open ball]]s of radius less than or equal to {{mvar|r}} with which it is possible to [[open cover|cover]] the set {{mvar|E}}.  The Assouad dimension of {{mvar|E}} is defined to be the [[infimum|infimal]] <math>\alpha \ge 0</math> for which there exist positive constants {{mvar|C}} and <math>\rho</math> so that, whenever
<math display="block">0 < r < R \leq \rho,</math>
the following bound holds:
<math display="block">\sup_{x \in E} N_{r}(B_{R}(x) \cap E) \leq C \left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^{\alpha}.</math>

The intuition underlying this definition is that, for a set {{mvar|E}} with "ordinary" integer dimension {{mvar|n}}, the number of small balls of radius {{mvar|r}} needed to cover the intersection of a larger ball of radius {{mvar|R}} with {{mvar|E}} will scale like {{math|(''R''/''r'')<sup>''n''</sup>}}.

==Relationships to other notions of dimension==
* The Assouad dimension of a metric space is always greater than or equal to its [[Assouad–Nagata dimension]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Le Donne |first1=Enrico |last2=Rajala |first2=Tapio |title=Assouad dimension, Nagata dimension, and uniformly close metric tangents |journal=[[Indiana University Mathematics Journal]] |date=2015 |volume=64 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1512/iumj.2015.64.5469 |arxiv=1306.5859|s2cid=55039643 }}</ref>
* The Assouad dimension of a metric space is always greater than or equal to its [[box-counting dimension|upper box dimension]], which in turn is greater than or equal to the [[Hausdorff dimension]].<ref name="Luukkainen"/>
* The [[Lebesgue covering dimension]] of a [[metrizable space]] {{mvar|X}} is the minimal Assouad dimension of any metric on {{mvar|X}}.  In particular, for every metrizable space there is a metric for which the Assouad dimension is equal to the Lebesgue covering dimension.<ref name="Luukkainen">{{cite journal |last1=Luukkainen |first1=Jouni |title=Assouad dimension: antifractal metrization, porous sets, and homogeneous measures |journal=Journal of the Korean Mathematical Society |date=1998 |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=23–76 |url=https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO199811919486026.page |issn=0304-9914}}</ref>
